summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for crash_2, grouped by per-hypothesis feature attribution.

mechanisms.description: In patients with viscoelastic evidence of hyperfibrinolysis, TXA stabilizes formed clots by inhibiting excessive plasmin‑mediated fibrin degradation, thereby reducing ongoing hemorrhage and 28‑day mortality.

In patients with fibrinolytic shutdown on VET, administration of TXA may exacerbate a prothrombotic balance by further suppressing residual fibrinolysis, increasing arterial and venous occlusive events.

Early administration of TXA during a transient hyperfibrinolytic window prevents progression to exsanguination, whereas VET‑guided delays that exceed the time‑sensitive window will diminish the mortality benefit observed in CRASH‑2.
Restricting TXA to VET‑confirmed hyperfibrinolysis reduces unnecessary drug exposure and thereby lowers incidence of TXA‑associated adverse events such as seizures linked to higher drug exposure.

VET‑guided TXA reduces 24‑hour blood product transfusion requirements by identifying patients whose bleeding is driven by fibrinolysis and who will achieve quicker clot stability after antifibrinolytic therapy.
Withholding TXA in non‑hyperfibrinolytic patients reduces formation of microvascular thrombi that would otherwise impair organ perfusion and contribute to multi‑organ failure.

Heterogeneous device‑specific thresholds for hyperfibrinolysis can lead to misclassification, causing some patients who would benefit to be denied TXA or others to receive unnecessary TXA, thus altering observed mortality and thrombotic rates.
Measured reductions in fibrinolysis biomarkers (for example, falling D‑dimer and plasmin–antiplasmin complexes) after TXA in VET‑positive patients will mediate reduced bleeding and transfusion needs.
In the VET‑guided strategy, rapid identification of hyperfibrinolysis permits targeted early TXA that synergizes with hemostatic interventions to shorten time to definitive hemostasis.

Administering TXA late within the guideline window to patients whose fibrinolytic profile has shifted toward shutdown may tip the haemostatic balance toward thrombosis and increase major vascular events.

VET‑based selection reduces biological heterogeneity of response to TXA across centers by ensuring treatment is given when active fibrinolysis is present, thereby increasing the observable treatment effect on bleeding outcomes.

Correlations between biobanked TXA levels and fibrinolysis markers will show that clinical benefit depends on both adequate drug exposure and pre‑treatment hyperfibrinolytic phenotype, supporting a pharmacodynamic mechanism.

In the VET‑with‑rescue operational arm, effect dilution will occur because some non‑hyperfibrinolytic patients receive TXA when assays fail, attenuating differences in vascular event rates between trial arms.
Systematically withholding TXA in VET‑negative patients reduces downstream transfusion‑related complications and ICU length of stay mediated by fewer transfusions and fewer thrombotic events.

Targeting TXA with point‑of‑care VET will change the balance between bleeding control and thrombotic risk at the population level, resulting in lower net morbidity by aligning antifibrinolytic therapy with individual coagulation phenotypes.
